messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla, a meticulous and respected auditor of 63, had built her life on logic and predictable outcomes. For forty years, her work had been to find patterns, assess risks, and impose order on chaos. Now, her own mind was a landscape of unpredictable terror, a place she could no longer audit or control. The shift began nine months ago, on a hiking trip in a narrow slot canyon with her partner, Omar. They were admiring the ancient sandstone walls when a low rumble escalated into a roar. The rockslide was sudden and absolute. Layla was thrown clear, but Omar was caught, his leg pinned by a boulder in a small alcove. For hours, she had stayed with him, her voice echoing in the confined space as she promised help was coming. She remembers the smell of dust and damp earth, the chilling feel of the rock against her cheek as she tried to listen for his breathing, and then, the silence that fell long before the rescue team arrived.

Now, the canyon is no longer a memory; it is a constant, lurking possibility. The trauma lives not in the past but in the present, ambushing her without warning. A few weeks ago, at work, a junior colleague closed the door to the small, windowless records room they were in. The solid click of the lock was all it took. Instantly, Layla was no longer in her office building; she was back in the suffocating darkness of the canyon, the terror of that day washing over her with the force of a physical blow. When the memory comes, it feels completely real, a full sensory reliving that brings with it the same frantic helplessness she felt as Omar’s voice grew weaker. This experience solidified a belief that had been growing in her for months: her own body had become an enemy, reacting as if she were still in danger even when she was logically safe.

This profound sense of betrayal by her own nervous system fuels a pervasive state of threat. Layla has come to believe she is fundamentally helpless, that she has no power to stop bad things from happening. This conviction dictates her every action. She is constantly on guard, scanning rooms for exits, flinching at sudden noises. The hypervigilance is exhausting, leaving her unable to sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. Lying awake in the dark, her mind races, replaying scenarios, and this state of high alert makes her even more susceptible to the memories that wait at the edge of her consciousness. Her world has shrunk; she avoids any unfamiliar place where she cannot fully assess the danger in advance, a practice that is now threatening the job she once loved.

The components of her distress have locked into a brutal, self-sustaining cycle. Her belief in her own helplessness makes her scan the world for danger, and this state of hypervigilance makes her hypersensitive to triggers. She now perceives the world through a lens of imminent threat, which means a locked door or even a documentary about national parks is no longer neutral. These triggers, in turn, unleash the memories in their full sensory horror. Each time she is ambushed by the past, it serves as fresh, visceral proof of her core beliefs: that she is powerless, that the world is unsafe, and that she has lost all faith in a life that could contain such random cruelty. The terror of the recall reinforces her hypervigilance, and the cycle tightens. She can feel it happening—the more watchful she is, the more she finds things to be frightened of; the more she remembers, the more certain she is that she is broken.

Her refusal to travel to new client sites, a core function of her senior auditor role, has led to a difficult conversation with her manager. He was kind but firm; the company needed her to be able to do her job. That conversation was the final impetus for seeking help. Layla sits in the therapy room, her posture rigid, her hands clenched. What brought her here was the threat to her career, but what she is most afraid of is not losing her job. She is terrified that this internal state—the constant watchfulness, the sensory ambushes, the crushing weight of her own helplessness—is permanent. She is trapped not in a canyon of rock and earth, but in a prison of her own mind, and she is desperate to find a way out.
